verses.text: After the death of Joshua, the children of Israel asked of Yahweh,  saying, “Who should go up for us first against the Canaanites, to fight against them?”
Yahweh said, “Judah shall go up. Behold,  I have delivered the land into his hand.”
Judah said to Simeon his brother, “Come up with me into my lot, that we may fight against the Canaanites; and I likewise will go with you into your lot.” So Simeon went with him.
Judah went up, and Yahweh delivered the Canaanites and the Perizzites into their hand. They struck ten thousand men in Bezek.
They found Adoni-Bezek in Bezek, and they fought against him. They struck the Canaanites and the Perizzites.
But Adoni-Bezek fled. They pursued him, caught him, and cut off his thumbs and his big toes.
Adoni-Bezek said, “Seventy kings, having their thumbs and their big toes cut off, scavenged under my table. As I have done, so God  has done to me.” They brought him to Jerusalem, and he died there.
The children of Judah fought against Jerusalem, took it, struck it with the edge of the sword, and set the city on fire.
After that, the children of Judah went down to fight against the Canaanites who lived in the hill country, and in the South, and in the lowland.
Judah went against the Canaanites who lived in Hebron. (The name of Hebron before that was Kiriath Arba.) They struck Sheshai, Ahiman, and Talmai.
From there he went against the inhabitants of Debir. (The name of Debir before that was Kiriath Sepher.)
Caleb said, “I will give Achsah my daughter as wife to the man who strikes Kiriath Sepher, and takes it.”
Othniel the son of Kenaz, Caleb’s younger brother, took it, so he gave him Achsah his daughter as his wife.
When she came, she got him to ask her father for a field. She dismounted from off of her donkey; and Caleb said to her, “What would you like?”
She said to him, “Give me a blessing; because you have set me in the land of the South, give me also springs of water.” Then Caleb gave her the upper springs and the lower springs.

The children of the Kenite, Moses’ brother-in-law, went up out of the city of palm trees with the children of Judah into the wilderness of Judah, which is in the south of Arad; and they went and lived with the people.
Judah went with Simeon his brother, and they struck the Canaanites who inhabited Zephath, and utterly destroyed it. The name of the city was called Hormah.
Also Judah took Gaza with its border, and Ashkelon with its border, and Ekron with its border.
Yahweh was with Judah; and drove out the inhabitants of the hill country; for he could not drive out the inhabitants of the valley, because they had chariots of iron.
They gave Hebron to Caleb, as Moses had said, and he drove the three sons of Anak out of there.
The children of Benjamin did not drive out the Jebusites who inhabited Jerusalem, but the Jebusites dwell with the children of Benjamin in Jerusalem to this day.
The house of Joseph also went up against Bethel, and Yahweh was with them.
The house of Joseph sent to spy out Bethel. (The name of the city before that was Luz.)
The watchers saw a man come out of the city, and they said to him, “Please show us the entrance into the city, and we will deal kindly with you.”
He showed them the entrance into the city, and they struck the city with the edge of the sword; but they let the man and all his family go.
The man went into the land of the Hittites, built a city, and called its name Luz, which is its name to this day.

Manasseh did not drive out the inhabitants of Beth Shean and its towns, nor Taanach and its towns, nor the inhabitants of Dor and its towns, nor the inhabitants of Ibleam and its towns, nor the inhabitants of Megiddo and its towns; but the Canaanites would dwell in that land.
When Israel had grown strong, they put the Canaanites to forced labor, and did not utterly drive them out.
Ephraim didn’t drive out the Canaanites who lived in Gezer, but the Canaanites lived in Gezer among them.
Zebulun didn’t drive out the inhabitants of Kitron, nor the inhabitants of Nahalol; but the Canaanites lived among them, and became subject to forced labor.
Asher didn’t drive out the inhabitants of Acco, nor the inhabitants of Sidon, nor of Ahlab, nor of Achzib, nor of Helbah, nor of Aphik, nor of Rehob;
but the Asherites lived among the Canaanites, the inhabitants of the land; for they did not drive them out.

Naphtali didn’t drive out the inhabitants of Beth Shemesh, nor the inhabitants of Beth Anath; but he lived among the Canaanites, the inhabitants of the land. Nevertheless the inhabitants of Beth Shemesh and of Beth Anath became subject to forced labor.
The Amorites forced the children of Dan into the hill country, for they would not allow them to come down to the valley;
but the Amorites would dwell in Mount Heres, in Aijalon, and in Shaalbim. Yet the hand of the house of Joseph prevailed, so that they became subject to forced labor.
The border of the Amorites was from the ascent of Akrabbim, from the rock, and upward.

footnotes.content: After Joshua's death, Israel turns to the Lord with a humble question. There is no panic, no reaching for a new commander—they ask Yahweh directly who should lead. It's the posture we need when an era ends: not self-reliance, but a simple, honest "What now, Lord?"
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yahweh answers decisively: Judah first, and victory is already given—not promised, but *delivered*. The word lands like a benediction. The Lord does not send His people into uncertainty; He sends them into His already-conquered territory.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Judah does not hoard the victory. He invites his brother Simeon into the battle, pledging mutual aid—"I will go with you into *your* lot." This is covenant thinking: we rise or fall together, our victories belong to the whole family.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ten thousand men struck in Bezek—a place name that holds Judah's first great battle. Yahweh's hand is named plainly: *He delivered* the Canaanites and Perizzites. The victory is real, the divine hand is clear, and Judah's courage met it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Adoni-Bezek is found and engaged—the king of the land stands against Israel. Every step of conquest is a real fight, not a walk. The enemy has a name, a face, a will to resist.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Caught and maimed—thumbs and big toes cut off, leaving him helpless. This is brutal, and the text does not flinch from it. In that time, a king's defeat was total, his power unmade.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Adoni-Bezek's words ring with a terrible clarity: "As I have done, so God has done to me." He recognizes divine justice in his own end—he sits at his table having done the same to seventy kings, and now it is done to him. He dies in Jerusalem, acknowledging the hand that cut him down.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jerusalem burns. Judah takes the city with sword and fire—a turning point. Yet later we'll see how incomplete this triumph becomes. Victory and compromise will walk hand in hand through this whole book.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: After Jerusalem, Judah turns south and inland—the hill country, the South, the lowland. Each terrain is named, each campaign deliberate. Judah advances methodically, claiming the land promised to them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hebron, once called Kiriath Arba, was the city where Abraham walked and buried his dead. Now Judah drives out the three sons of Anak—giants of the old world—and reclaims a place drenched in covenant memory.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Debir, once Kiriath Sepher (the city of books or scribes), is next on Judah's path. The old names cling to these places like old letters; to conquer them is to rewrite history.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Caleb makes an ancient bargain: his daughter Achsah will go to the man who takes Kiriath Sepher. It is not cruelty but custom—a prize, a covenant sealed by marriage. Caleb trusts the Lord will provide the warrior.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Othniel, Caleb's younger brother, steps forward and claims the city—and the bride. Here is the first hint of the next judge; God's hand moves quietly beneath the surface, placing His servants in the arena.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Achsah comes to Othniel as wife, then immediately speaks. She dismounts and asks her father for one thing more—not for herself, but for the household. There is steel in her gentleness; she knows what a bride's portion should be.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Give me a blessing," she says—the Hebrew word *beraka* carries weight. She doesn't beg; she asks with the authority of a daughter. Caleb gives her upper springs and lower springs: he gives her abundance, not just survival.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Kenites, Moses' brother-in-law's people, go up with Judah from the city of palm trees (Jericho). They settle in the southern wilderness—a covenant family joining God's covenant people, finding their home in Judah's inheritance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Judah and Simeon together strike Zephath and utterly destroy it—then rename it Hormah (desolation). When a place is so thoroughly cleansed, its very name must change. It is a radical break with the past.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gaza, Ashkelon, Ekron—cities of the Philistines, great coastal strongholds—fall to Judah. The tribal inheritance moves to its borders. But Gaza especially will prove a persistent thorn; nothing is truly settled here.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yahweh was with Judah in the mountains, but iron chariots held the valleys. Here is the first crack in the story: not failure, but incompleteness. Judah did what it could, but the promise required more faith, or more time.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hebron is given to Caleb as Moses said—a seventy-year-old man finally receiving what was sworn to him in the wilderness. The three sons of Anak, giants of terror, are driven out. Faithfulness is crowned.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Benjamin does not drive out the Jebusites from Jerusalem, so they dwell together "to this day." This note whispers a warning: the half-measures of one generation become the bondage of the next.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joseph's house goes up against Bethel, and Yahweh is with them. The northern tribes move, and the divine favor moves with them. But again, we are watching obedience tested in real time.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Bethel, once called Luz, held a sacred memory—Jacob's ladder vision. Now Joseph's spies go to scout it. The old name clings to it; sacred places bear witness to what they have seen.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A man comes out of the city, and Israel makes a covenant with him: show us the way, and we will show you mercy. Even in conquest, there is room for mercy toward one who chooses it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He shows them the entrance; they strike the city with the sword, but his whole household is spared. He kept faith with Israel, and Israel kept faith with him. Mercy shown to the merciful.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The man departs to the land of the Hittites and builds a city, calling it Luz. He carries the old name into a new land, a new exile—a survivor bearing witness, building again elsewhere.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Manasseh does not drive out Beth Shean, Taanach, Dor, Ibleam, Megiddo—a long catalogue of failure to fully possess. The Lord gave the inheritance, but the people did not finish the work.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When Israel grew strong, they put the Canaanites to labor but did not drive them out entirely. Strength used for subjugation instead of cleansing—a pattern that will haunt this generation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ephraim too failed to drive out the Canaanites of Gezer; they lived among them. Another failure, another tribe settling for compromise. The inheritance is there, but the will to claim it fully is not.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Zebulun did not drive out Kitron or Nahalol; the Canaanites lived among them under forced labor. It is the same sad pattern: settlement without cleansing, coexistence without covenant clarity.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Asher did not drive out Acco, Sidon, Ahlab, Achzib, Helbah, Aphik, Rehob—a whole coastal territory left unconquered. Each name is a city left to its own gods.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Asherites lived among the Canaanites, for they did not drive them out. The formula is now fixed in the reader's mind: we did not. We did not. We did not.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Naphtali also failed to drive out Beth Shemesh and Beth Anath; they lived among the Canaanites. Yet these inhabitants were made subject to forced labor—a half-victory that breeds resentment, not peace.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Amorites forced the children of Dan into the hill country, denying them the valley. Here is a reversal: not Israel conquering, but Israel pushed back, hemmed in. The gap between promise and possession widens.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Amorites held Mount Heres, Aijalon, Shaalbim, until Joseph's hand prevailed and they too became servants. Yet the fact that it took force to reduce them shows they never should have remained at all.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The border of the Amorites runs from Akrabbim upward—a line drawn but not erased. Readers today hear an echo: how many borders do we accept in our own hearts, lines where we chose comfort over obedience? Looking back from 2026, I see the Lord calling us still to finish what He began.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
